  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE

  rename(area_id = MSOA21CD) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(area_id)

  file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

spatial_graph <- file.path(base_path, "clean", "msoa_queen.adj")
When detailed population counts are available for combinations of predictors used in a unit-level SAE model, poststratification can provide a fuller representation of the target population. It combines a model fitted to survey microdata with a poststratification table, then aggregates predictions across population cells using their population counts. This is the core principle of what is commonly known Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP).

title: Unit-level SAE with poststratification (MRP)
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome: Share of adults who cycle for transport several times weekly
Spatial: MSOAs in Wales
Temporal: Over three survey periods 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025




For this estimand, we model the binary frequent-cycling indicator, freq_cyclist, using age_band, sex, caraccess, and spatial and temporal random effects in a generalised linear mixed model. We predict the outcome for every age_band × sex × caraccess cell, then aggregate these predictions to MSOA-year estimates using the corresponding population counts. Repeating this aggregation across posterior draws propagates uncertainty into the estimates.
The poststratification table is derived from the most recent UK census, giving the 2021 population count for each age_band × sex × caraccess cell within each MSOA. The model can estimate different outcomes for the 2023 and 2025 survey waves through its temporal and spatial effects, but the poststratification weights remain fixed at their 2021 values. This assumes that local age, sex, and car-access composition does not drastically change across survey years, or N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021}.
The unit-level models do not incorporate survey weights in the likelihood. This relies on the assumption that, after conditioning on the fixed and random effects, survey inclusion is independent of frequent cycling.

2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit binomial unit-level models to the survey microdata, then use them to predict area-time means. We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:



Model
Name
Specification




M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+Demographic
M1 plus age band and sex


M3
+CarAccess
M2 plus respondent car access




m1_formula <- freq_cyclist ~
  1 +
  f(
    time_inla_id, 
    model = "rw1", 
    scale.model = TRUE
    ) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph,
    scale.model = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  age_band +
  sex
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . + 
  caraccess
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)


fit_mrp_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    data = model_data,
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_mrp_model)

title: Unit-level SAE with poststratification (MRP)
text:
3 Poststratification with posterior draws
As before, posterior draws from the selected R-INLA fit produce MSOA-year estimates. Each draw provides fixed effects, spatial area effects, and temporal effects. The fitted model is evaluated over every age_band x sex x caraccess population cell, transformed to the response scale, weighted by pop_count, and summarised as MSOA-year draws.






Why poststratification?



The unit-level model is fitted to survey microdata, but the survey sample may not match the target population composition (see below figure). Poststratification partially adjusts this by predicting the outcome for known population groups and weighting those predictions by the corresponding population counts. This helps align the estimates with the population structure (but only for the variables included in the poststratification table).








set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = mrp_final_fit
)

Each posterior draw is evaluated over every poststratification cell.

extract_draws <- function(posterior_draws, nodes, row_names = nodes) {
  matrix(
    sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) draw$latent[nodes, 1]),
    nrow = length(nodes),
    dimnames = list(row_names, NULL)
  )
}

predict_from_draws <- function(posterior_draws, prediction_data, fixed_term_formula) {
  # Build prediction matrix
  prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
    fixed_term_formula,
    prediction_data
  )
  
  # Extract draws of fixed and spatial/temporal effect from posteriors
  fixed_terms <- colnames(prediction_matrix)
  area_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$area_inla_id))
  time_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$time_inla_id))

  fixed_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"))
  area_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids))
  time_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids))

  # Calculate the linear predictor and convert to probabilities
  linear_predictor <- prediction_matrix %*% fixed_draws +
    area_draws[match(prediction_data$area_inla_id, area_ids), ] +
    time_draws[match(prediction_data$time_inla_id, time_ids), ]

  plogis(linear_predictor)
}

cell_draws <- predict_from_draws(
  posterior_draws,
  poststrat_data,
  ~ age_band + sex + caraccess
)

The cell predictions are then ‘poststratified’`, i.e., weighted by population count and aggregated within each MSOA-year.

poststratify <- function(cell_draws, weights, area, time) {
  area_time <- paste(area, time, sep = "__")
  weighted_predictions <- rowsum(cell_draws * weights, group = area_time)
  population_totals <- rowsum(weights, group = area_time)
  weighted_predictions / as.numeric(population_totals)
}

prediction_draws <- poststratify(
  cell_draws,
  weights = poststrat_data$pop_count,
  area = poststrat_data$area_id,
  time = poststrat_data$time_id
)

The matrix prediction_draws now has one MSOA-year estimate per row and one posterior draw per column. Posterior means, variances, and 95% credible intervals are computed directly from this draw matrix.

final_mrp_results <- tibble(
  area_year_id = rownames(prediction_draws)
) |>
  separate(
    area_year_id,
    into = c("area_id", "time_id"),
    sep = "__",
    convert = TRUE
  ) |>
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      mrp_estimate = rowMeans(prediction_draws),
      mrp_variance = apply(prediction_draws, 1, var),
      mrp_lower = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      mrp_upper = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    mrp_ci_width = mrp_upper - mrp_lower
  )

text:
Code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
output_path <- here::here("outputs")
dir.create(output_path, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = MSOA21CD) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(area_id)

  file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

The previous direct-estimation results show that survey coverage is often too sparse and uneven to support reliable MSOA-year estimates of frequent cycling behaviour on their own. Once a model-based approach is needed, area-level SAE is a logical next step because it builds directly on the direct estimates already produced, modelling these estimates with their sampling variances and area-level auxiliary data to improve precision while retaining the survey evidence.

title: Area-level SAE
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome: Share of adults who cycle for transport several times weekly
Spatial: MSOAs in Wales
Temporal: Over three survey periods 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025




In a Fay–herriot style area-level SAE model, each direct estimate for an MSOA–year cell is treated as a noisy measurement of the underlying frequent-cycling rate. Its sampling variance determines how much weight the model gives to the local survey evidence.
The model combines MSOA-level predictors (average age, population density, share of residents with access to a car, etc.) with spatial and temporal random effects to share information across areas and survey years. Where direct evidence is strong, the estimate remains close to the direct estimate. Where it is weak or unavailable, the estimate relies more heavily on the predictors and random effects.

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because this controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the area-level model.

For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be determined by the model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for cycling frequently, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.


max_variance <- max(direct_bike$variance[direct_bike$variance > 0], na.rm = TRUE)

direct_bike <- direct_bike |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(variance) ~ max_variance,
      variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ variance
    )
  )

Finally, we assemble the modelling data for R-INLA by combining the direct estimates with the area predictors and the imported numeric indices for the temporal and spatial effects.

2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to R-INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using R-INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
+iid
Independent, unstructured area effects; no temporal effect or spatial smoothing.


M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal and spatial effect


M2
+AvgAge
M1 plus mean adult age


M3
+PopdensCaraccess
M2 plus population density and share of adults with car access



The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.







Temporal model
Description




rw1
First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods.


rw2
Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series.


ar1
Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years.










Spatial model
Description




iid
Unstructured area-level variation.


besag
Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation.


bym
Combines a structured Besag component with an unstructured iid component.


bym2
A reparameterised BYM model with a mixing parameter, phi, which represents the proportion of residual variation that is spatially structured.



With only three survey years, rw1 is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, bym2 is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "iid"
  )

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph,
    scale.model = TRUE
  ) +
  f(
    time_inla_id, 
    model = "rw1", 
    scale.model = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . + 
  z_age_adult_mean
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  z_pop_density +
  z_caraccess_adult_share
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 +iid" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +AvgAge" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +PopdensCaraccess" = m3_formula
)


fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When fitting area-level SAE models with R-INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the estimates for each area-time row.
scale passes the inverse sampling variance, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
control.family fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.



Model fit is compared with WAIC (Widely Applicable Information Criterion), a global predictive-fit measure returned by R-INLA. Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
    )
  }
) |>
  arrange(waic)

title: Area-level SAE
text:
3 Estimation with posterior draws
Posterior draws from the selected R-INLA fit give area-level SAE estimates for each MSOA-year cell. The fitted-value draws are summarised into the posterior mean, variance, and 95% credible interval.

set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = fh_selected_fit
)

Each posterior draw is evaluated for each MSOA-year domain by plugging in the area-level predictor summaries and the corresponding area and time effects.

extract_draws <- function(posterior_draws, nodes, row_names = nodes) {
  matrix(
    sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) draw$latent[nodes, 1]),
    nrow = length(nodes),
    dimnames = list(row_names, NULL)
  )
}

predict_from_draws <- function(posterior_draws, prediction_data, fixed_term_formula) {
  # Build prediction matrix
  prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
    fixed_term_formula,
    prediction_data
  )

  # Extract fixed and random effects into a matrix
  fixed_terms <- colnames(prediction_matrix)
  area_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$area_inla_id))
  time_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$time_inla_id))

  fixed_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"))
  area_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids))
  time_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids))

  # Calculate fitted value for each draw
  prediction_matrix %*% fixed_draws +
    area_draws[match(prediction_data$area_inla_id, area_ids), ] +
    time_draws[match(prediction_data$time_inla_id, time_ids), ]
}

prediction_draws <- predict_from_draws(
  posterior_draws,
  model_data,
  ~ z_age_adult_mean
)







Alternative: extract predictions directly from R-INLA



In the code above, for each posterior draw, we construct predictions for each MSOA-year from the fixed and random effects manually. R-INLA performs the same calculation during model fitting, and control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) retains the resulting linear predictors as Predictor: values. Because the model uses an identity link—i.e., no conversion is applied, a fitted value of 0.08 represents an 8% prevalence—the prediction draws can therefore be extracted directly:

prediction_draws <- sapply(
  posterior_draws,
  \(draw) draw$latent[startsWith(rownames(draw$latent), "Predictor:"), 1]
)



The matrix prediction_draws has one MSOA-year estimate per row and one posterior draw per column. Posterior means, variances, and 95% credible intervals are computed directly from this draw matrix.

final_fh_results <- model_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id) |>
  bind_cols(

      fh_estimate = rowMeans(prediction_draws),
      fh_variance = apply(prediction_draws, 1, var),
      fh_lower = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      fh_upper = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)

  ) |>
  mutate(
    fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower

title: Bayesian Spatiotemporal Small-area Estimation with R-INLA
text:
1 Small-area Estimation in Urban Analytics

1.1 What is small-area estimation?
Urban researchers rely on surveys to understand different aspects of the target populations and how they change over time, often examining survey results at different spatial scales–such as neighbourhoods, census blocks, or transport zones–to compare places, track local trends, and identify inequalities. A key challenge is that simply grouping survey responses by area can leave too few respondents to produce reliable estimates, while combining responses from several survey years can obscure changes over time and introduce bias if differences between years are not properly accounted for. Another challenge is deciding which SAE modelling and prediction method suitable for their data constraints and research questions.
This guide introduces several Bayesian spatiotemporal small area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics–with implementation in R-INLA–to help researchers choose a method suited to their data limitations using an illustrative case study of frequent cycling behaviour in Wales.


1.2 Bayesian inference and R-INLA
While frequentist methods typically use a prediction formula and an estimated mean squared error (MSE) to quantify uncertainty, Bayesian approaches treat model parameters as probability distributions. Each posterior draw gives one possible set of parameter values, and recalculating the domain estimate for every draw produces a posterior distribution of plausible estimates. Its mean is the reported estimate, while its spread and quantiles describe uncertainty.
This carries uncertainty from all model components into the estimates and supports complex spatiotemporal models.



Bayesian inference combines survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, relationships between neighbouring areas, temporal dependence and uncertainty from sparse domains within a joint probability model.


The workbooks use R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). This method provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models and is faster than Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for complex spatiotemporal small area estimation models.

title: Survey data
text:
1 About the survey
The analysis uses a harmonised dataset of three waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW): 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025. The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language.
The raw survey geography and stratification variable is Local Authority. In this guide, each respondent is assigned to a synthetic MSOA within their Local Authority using random allocation. This serves two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution. The synthetic MSOA assignment supports MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and unit-level SAE with poststratification.
Privacy. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



In the UK, Local Authorities (LAs) are administrative areas responsible for local government, also referred to as unitary authorities in Wales. Middle Layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs) are smaller statistical areas used to report census and other official statistics in England and Wales. Each contains about 2,000–6,000 households and 5,000–15,000 residents, and lies within a single Local Authority.

2 Preparation steps for small-area estimation

2.1 Target Estimand
The target estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It defines the outcome, population, geography, time period, and the auxiliary data needed for modelling, such as predictors or population counts, and can be articulated in the following format. Note that the most common outcomes to estimate are means of continuous variables and prevalence—expressed as shares or proportions—within the target population.
In this guide, our target estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome: Share of adults who cycle for transport several times weekly
Spatial: MSOAs in Wales
Temporal: Over three survey periods 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025






2.2 Estimation Domains
In spatio-temporal SAE, the estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination forms an area-time cell for which an estimate is required. The estimation domains are the complete set of these cells.
For the estimand defined above, the estimation domains therefore include every MSOA–year combination, including cells with no survey observations.

Direct estimation is the starting point for the SAE workflow. 2 Calculate direct estimates
svyby() computes the weighted share and uncertainty diagnostics for every area-time cell with usable observations. The completed area-by-time grid retains missing cells for later modelling.

# Define survey design
bike_design <- svydesign(
  ids = ~1,
  strata = ~strata,
  weights = ~weight,
  data = survey_bike
)

# Calculate direct estimate and uncertainty
direct_bike_estimates <- svyby(
  formula = ~freq_cyclist,
  by = ~area_id + time_id,
  design = bike_design,
  FUN = svymean,
  vartype = "se",
  na.rm = TRUE,
  keep.names = FALSE
) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_estimate = freq_cyclist,
    variance = se^2
  )

# Calculate sample size per area-time cell
direct_bike_counts <- survey_bike |>
  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Join together
direct_bike <- domain_frame |>
  left_join(direct_bike_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  left_join(direct_bike_counts, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(n = replace_na(n, 0L))

3 Assess precision and coverage
Direct estimation provides a useful starting point because it makes three limitations visible:

Uneven coverage: The number of usable observations varies across survey waves and MSOAs, leaving some area-time cells with much less direct evidence than others.
Unstable area estimates over time: For some MSOAs, direct estimates change sharply between waves, which may reflect real change or simply sampling noise.
Invalid variances: Since freq_cyclist is a binary indicator, all respondents in an area with a small sample size may give the same response. The estimated sampling variance is then zero, incorrectly suggesting that the prevalence estimate has no uncertainty. For all intents and purposes, these small-area estimates are unusable for further analysis.

Sparse and uneven survey coverage at the target MSOA-year scale limits how far direct estimates can be reported on their own. This motivates the use of model-based SAE methods that borrow strength across areas, years, and auxiliary predictors to produce more stable estimates with appropriately quantified uncertainty.
Two model-based options follow:

Area-level SAE stabilises direct MSOA-year estimates using sampling variances to control how much weight each direct estimate receives (Fay–Herriot model).
Unit-level SAE estimates the individual outcome from survey microdata and aggregates predictions to target MSOA-years.

The choice between area-level and unit-level modelling should depend on the quality of the direct estimates and sampling variances as model inputs, and whether the survey microdata contain unit-level predictors that explain variation in the freq_cyclist binary indicator.
In this example, the summary points to important limitations for area-level modelling since there are many domains with invalid variances. Nonetheless, we still fit an area-level model at the next workbook first to show how much stabilisation is possible from direct-estimate inputs before moving to unit-level modelling.

title: Unit-level SAE with predictor summaries
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome: Share of adults who cycle for transport several times weekly
Spatial: MSOAs in Wales
Temporal: Over three survey periods 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025




There are several unit-level SAE frameworks. This guide uses a generalised linear mixed model inspired by the Battese–Harter–Fuller model. It models individual continuous or binary outcomes using predictors available in the survey microdata. Final small-area estimates are produced by applying the fitted model to area-level summaries of those predictors.
Here, the binary freq_cyclist indicator is modelled using temporal and spatial random effects. The model specifications progressively add the unit-level predictors age, sex, and caraccess. Aggregation with predictor summaries assumes that these summaries adequately represent the target population in each MSOA-year cell.
The unit-level models do not incorporate survey weights in the likelihood. This relies on the assumption that, after conditioning on the fixed and random effects, survey inclusion is independent of frequent cycling.

We fit binomial unit-level models to the survey microdata, then use them to predict area-time means. We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:

Name
Specifications

  1 +
  f(
    time_inla_id, 
    model = "rw1", 
    scale.model = TRUE
  ) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph,
    scale.model = TRUE

  age +
  female
)

  caraccess
)

  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula

    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    data = model_data,
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)

}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)

title: Unit-level SAE with predictor summaries
section: 3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
text:
3 Estimation and aggregation with posterior draws
The aggregation step uses posterior draws from the selected R-INLA fit to produce unit-level SAE estimates for each MSOA-year cell. We first sample from the posterior and extract the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect. We then rebuild the fitted model for every MSOA-year aggregation row and summarise the resulting draws.

set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = bhf_selected_fit
)

Each posterior draw is evaluated over the MSOA-year aggregation frame by plugging in the area-level predictor summaries and the corresponding area and time effects.

extract_draws <- function(posterior_draws, nodes, row_names = nodes) {
  matrix(
    sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) draw$latent[nodes, 1]),
    nrow = length(nodes),
    dimnames = list(row_names, NULL)
  )
}
predict_from_draws <- function(posterior_draws, prediction_data, fixed_term_formula) {
  
  # Build prediction matrix
  prediction_matrix <- model.matrix(
    fixed_term_formula,
    prediction_data
  )

  # Extract draws of fixed and spatial/temporal effect from posteriors
  fixed_terms <- colnames(prediction_matrix)
  area_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$area_inla_id))
  time_ids <- sort(unique(prediction_data$time_inla_id))

  fixed_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"))
  area_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids))
  time_draws <- extract_draws(posterior_draws,paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids))

  # Calculate the linear predictor and convert to probabilities
  linear_predictor <- prediction_matrix %*% fixed_draws +
    area_draws[match(prediction_data$area_inla_id, area_ids), ] +
    time_draws[match(prediction_data$time_inla_id, time_ids), ]

  plogis(linear_predictor)
}

prediction_draws <- predict_from_draws(
  posterior_draws,
  aggregation_data,
  ~ age + female + caraccess
)

The matrix prediction_draws now has one MSOA-year estimate per row and one posterior draw per column. Posterior means, variances, and 95% credible intervals are computed directly from this draw matrix.

final_bhf_results <- aggregation_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id) |>
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      bhf_estimate = rowMeans(prediction_draws),
      bhf_variance = apply(prediction_draws, 1, var),
      bhf_lower = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
      bhf_upper = apply(prediction_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    bhf_ci_width = bhf_upper - bhf_lower
  )

title: Unit-level SAE with predictor summaries
text:
4 Limitation for binary indicators
Although unit-level modelling can stabilise estimates where direct estimates are weak, aggregation using area-level predictor summaries still relies on strong assumptions about population composition. Representing age, sex, and car access using mean adult age, the adult female share, and the adult share with car access can conceal important differences in their joint distribution. Two areas may have similar marginal summaries but very different age–sex–car compositions, leading to similar model-based estimates even when cycling behaviour differs across particular population groups.
This limitation is especially important for a binary outcome modelled using a logistic model (setting family = "binomial"). The target is the population-average predicted probability. Substituting area-level predictor summaries to estimate the probability at the average predictor values only is an approximation.






Area summaries and binary outcomes



For continuous outcomes, such as commute time in minutes, substituting area-level predictor summaries into a linear model gives the same result as averaging individual predictions:

\bar{x}\beta
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\beta

For binary outcomes, such as freq_cyclist (1 = yes, 0 = no), the target is the population proportion in the area, or the average predicted probability across individuals. Plugging in area-level summaries instead gives the predicted probability for an “average” individual, so it is only an approximation to the target.

\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\bar{x}\beta)
\approx
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(x_i\beta)



A poststratification table addresses this limitation by providing population counts for the joint combinations of the relevant predictors. This is the logic of multilevel regression with poststratification (MRP): predict the outcome for each population cell, then aggregate the cell predictions using the corresponding population counts so that the estimate reflects the composition of the target population.

title: Cross method comparison
text:
We can now compare the direct estimates and three model-based SAE approaches developed in the preceding sections in order to show how each approach changes the estimates, and their uncertainty. The comparison serve to illustrate the practical trade-offs that researchers should consider when selecting an approach for their own data and estimand.
The table below summarises the main data requirements, strengths, and limitations of each method.

title: Cross method comparison
text:
1 Smoothing and target population adjustment
The distribution and rank plots compare the spread of MSOA-year estimates across methods, while the maps compare the local pattern of estimated frequent cycling.

Direct estimates are highly uneven, while model-based estimates are smoother because they borrow strength across areas, years, predictors, or poststratification cells.
The area-level model is anchored by the direct estimates, so the strength of local survey evidence influences the modelled results. In 2025, which has the largest median sample size, the modelled estimates remain closer to the direct estimates. In the earlier waves with weaker direct evidence, the modelled estimates are much higher.
Differences between the estimates from the two unit-level models are more subtle because they use similar models and spatio-temporal structure. Their main difference is how the individual predictions are projected to the MSOA–year level.











In a unit-level SAE workflow, poststratification changes how the predicted population cells are aggregated. By examining the two MSOAs with the largest increase and decrease after adjusting to the Census population shares, we see that the Cardiff MSOA with higher proportions of groups that are more likely to be frequent cyclists (e.g., 16-49 males with no cars) sees an upward poststratified adjustment compared to the other where there are higher proportions of groups with lower probabilities (e.g., 50+ females with access to a car).

title: Cross method comparison
text:
2 Improvement in precision
Interval width summarises the uncertainty attached to each estimate. For direct estimates, interval width is driven by the sampling variance within each MSOA-year cell. Model-based approaches produce 95% credible intervals that reflect posterior uncertainty. Overall, we see a massive improvement in precision when employing a model-based SAE approach.










Narrower intervals can reflect improved precision, but they may also result from stronger smoothing and greater reliance on model-based estimates when local survey evidence is weak, as seen in the area-level model. In comparison, the marginally wider intervals from the unit-level models reflect their more fine-grained specification since here we are fitting the model over thousands of survey respondents.

title: Cross method comparison
text:
3 Examining spatial and temporal effects
Spatial and temporal random effects capture residual variation not explained by the fixed predictors. Their relative contribution can differ across SAE approaches because the models use the survey data in different ways.
We compare the posterior variance of the total BYM2 area effect and the RW1 temporal effect, expressed as inverse precision, 1/\tau. For RW1, it is the variance of the temporal effect across the three survey periods. For BYM2, this is the total residual area-effect variance, including structured (i.e., spatial variation explained by the neighbourhood structure) and unstructured components. Overall, the unit-level model has a larger spatial-effect variance (i.e., stronger spatial smoothing), although both models are provided with the same neighbourhood-based spatial weight matrix. Instead, the area-level model exhibits stronger temporal smoothing due to highly uneven estimates across years.





To examine the area effects in more detail, we distinguish between the structured and unstructured components of the BYM2 model suing the mixing parameter, \phi, i.e., the proportion of residual area-effect variance assigned to the spatially structured component. The closer to zero the greater the unstructured, area-specific effects not explainable by neighbouring areas.
The area-level model has a lower median \phi than the unit-level model. This indicates that residual area variation is more strongly unstructured in the area-level model, whereas the unit-level model identifies a stronger adjacency-based spatial pattern. This difference is consistent with sparse and unstable direct estimates providing limited information for identifying a coherent spatial pattern.





Overall, these results suggest that the area-level model gains little from including a spatial neighbourhood matrix, compared with the unit-level model. In practice, this means that although the research question may suggest spatial dependence and motivate spatial smoothing in SAE, this structure does not always add useful information. In such cases, an independent, unstructured area random effect may be sufficient.
